title: Friends and small talk
goals: Ask and answer personal questions with be and the simple present (Are you...? Do you...? Where does...?).
Talk about your family, home, work, and studies.
Find things in common: I do too, I don't either, Me too, Me neither.
Start a conversation with a stranger and use actually.
Talk about your free time, likes, and feelings.
Write with correct capital letters, commas, and question marks.

learn.title: Short questions and answers: be and the simple present
learn.html:
To get to know someone, you ask questions. With the verb be, you switch the order (be + subject). With other verbs, you need do / does as a helper, and the main verb stays in its base form.

QuestionShort answer
beAre you from a big family?Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
doDo you have any brothers or sisters?Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
doesDoes your brother work in a bank?Yes, he does. / No, he doesn't.
Wh- + beWhere are your parents from?They're from Peru.
Wh- + do/doesWhat does your brother do?He's a nurse.
  • Negatives: They aren't from Peru. / He doesn't work in a bank. (after doesn't, the verb has no -s).
  • The positive short answer is not contracted: Yes, I am. (not Yes, I'm).
  • What do you do? means what's your job?

watch.why: With be, don't use do: be + subject.
After doesn't, the verb has no -s.
The positive short answer with be is not contracted.

learn.title: Agreeing: too, either, me too, me neither
learn.html:
To say that you also do (or don't do) something, you repeat the helper verb from the sentence and add too (after a positive) or either (after a negative).

They say...You answer...
I'm allergic to cats.I am too. / Me too.
I'm not an animal lover.I'm not either. / Me neither.
I watch pro football.I do too. / Me too.
I don't watch much TV.I don't either. / Me neither. / Me either.
I can shop for hours.I can too.
I can't afford anything new.I can't either.

If you don't agree, say Really? and give your information: I don't watch sports. — Really? I watch all the basketball games.

  • Me too is only used after positives; Me neither is only used after negatives.
  • English doesn't use a double negative: I don't either, not I don't neither.

watch.wrong: I don't like cats. — I don't too.
watch.right: I don't like cats. — I don't either.
watch.why: After a negative, use either, not too.

watch.wrong: I'm not a morning person. — Me too.
watch.right: I'm not a morning person. — Me neither.

watch.why: Don't use two negatives: don't + either.

watch.wrong: I like jazz. — I like too.
watch.right: I like jazz. — I do too.
watch.why: Repeat the helper verb: I do too.

learn.title: Capital letters and punctuation
learn.html:
In English, punctuation follows different rules than in Spanish. These are the most useful ones for writing messages:

RuleExample
Capital letter for names, countries, languages, nationalities, days, and monthsMy friend Ana speaks English on Mondays.
Capital letter at the start of a sentence and for IDo you know where I live?
Comma in lists (before and)I like pizza, tacos, and burgers.
Comma before a quote or when you name someoneShe says, "Hello." / Nice to meet you, Mariana.
Period at the end of statementsKeep in touch.
Only one question mark, at the endAre you new to the company?
  • Possessive: my sister's name (one sister) / my sisters' names (several).
  • English has no opening question mark (¿) or exclamation mark (¡).

watch.why: English has no opening question mark (¿).
I and country names are capitalized.
Days and languages are capitalized in English.

watch.wrong: I like tacos pizza and burgers.
watch.right: I like tacos, pizza, and burgers.
watch.why: Separate the items of a list with commas.

learn.title: Small talk with a stranger and using actually
learn.html:
How to start a conversation with someone you don't know:

  • Comment on what you see or hear: It's cold tonight. / This is a great party, huh? / There are a lot of people here.
  • Ask a general question: Do you come here a lot?
  • Say your name: By the way, my name's Chris.

Actually does not mean “currently”; it means “in fact” or “really”. It is used for:

UseExample
Giving new informationYeah, I do, actually.
Giving surprising informationActually, I kind of like cold weather.
Correcting someone politely— So, you're American? — Well, actually, I'm from Canada.
  • Really? shows surprise or polite disagreement: I hate this weather. — Really? I love it!
  • Actually goes at the start, before the verb, or at the end: I teach skiing, actually.

write.prompt: Write a message of 60 to 100 words to someone you have just met: say where you live and with whom, what you do for a living, what you do in your free time, and ask two questions. Opening example: Hi! I'm Carlos and I live in Puebla...
checklist: Capital letters for names, cities, and I
Commas in lists and a question mark at the end

In my free time, I play soccer and I read comics. I don't watch much TV. My friends and I go to the cinema on Saturdays. Do you live in Mexico City? What do you do in your free time? reading.title: Sofia's first party at the language club
paragraphs: Sofia is 24 and she lives in Guadalajara. She isn't an only child: she has two brothers and one sister. She lives with her parents in a house near the center, and her brothers live nearby. Sofia works part-time in a software company, and she studies English at night. "I want to make new friends," she says, "because I don't have much free time."

On Saturday she goes to a party at her language club. It is freezing outside and there is a long line at the door. A boy next to her says, "It's cold tonight, huh?" "Yes, it is," says Sofia. "I'm a little nervous, actually. I don't know anyone here." The boy smiles. "Me neither! By the way, my name's Diego."

They start to talk. Diego is a full-time student and he works in a vintage store on weekends. "Do you have any pets?" asks Sofia. "No, I don't," says Diego. "I'm an animal lover, but I'm allergic to cats." "I am too!" says Sofia. "I have a dog, but I can't have a cat." They also learn that Diego doesn't watch much TV, and Sofia doesn't either. They both prefer documentaries and sports.

When the party ends, Diego asks, "Do you want to eat out tomorrow? I don't sleep late on Sundays." "Sure," says Sofia. "I'm not a morning person, actually, but I can wake up early!" She thinks it's easy to make friends when you smile, ask questions, and listen.

Nice to meet you, Tom. I'm Mia. Do you come to this club a lot?
No, I don't. Actually, it's my first time. My brother plays in the band.
Oh, really? Which one is he?
The lead singer. He's a full-time musician, and I work in a bank.
Cool. I work part-time in a vintage store, and I study art at night.
What do you do in your free time?
I eat out with friends and I play sports. I'm a big football fan.
Me too! I don't sleep late on Sundays because I play football in the park.
